To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) the perception of self-velocity and scene velocity is not continuous during the induction of vection and that (2) inertial motions with amplitudes above certain thresholds impair vection.

the induction of saturated yaw or surge vection requires 2-3 sec of constant angular or linear acceleration, respectively, that the induction of yaw or surge vections can be impaired by inertial motions that are perceived by the subject as additional self-motion, that the amplitudes of inertial motion required to impair saturated vection are greater for translations than for the rotations, and that the impairment of saturated vections is greater for yaw than for surge vection.

the perception of self-acceleration is not necessary for vection, that the perception of a sudden change in self-motion velocity is necessary for the induction of vection, that vection can be impaired when inertial motions are added to the vection inducing stimulus, and that the impairment is more robust for rotations than for translations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of inertial motions on the induction and impairment of vection.
the perception of self-acceleration and self-deceleration.
the effects of inertial motion on vection.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the subjects perceived the applied inertial movements, but that they did not perceive any additional self-motion during the induction of vection.
, in general, the perception of self-acceleration is not necessary for the induction of vection.
the subjects experienced a sudden change in self-motion during the induction of vection and that the subjects experienced additional self-motion during the impairment of vection.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the subjects were able to perceive the applied inertial forces and torques, but were not able to integrate the inertial motion with the vection motion to perceive the total self- and visual scene motion.

the perception of self-acceleration and visual scene decelerations is not necessary for the induction of vection and that the inertial motion amplitude required to impair vection is dependent on the type of motion.
the induction of vection is not affected by inertial motions, but that the perception of inertial motion is impaired by the induction of vections.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the perception of self-acceleration and visual scene decelerations during the induction of vection is not a prerequisite for the induction of vections.
the inertial motion am-plitudes that impair vection are close to those that are perceived as additional self-motion.
inertial motions can impair the perception of self-rotation and translation, but that the inertial motions needed for impairment are smaller for translations than for rotation.
